extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, and practitioners interested in misinformation, media literacy, and countermeasures
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes definitions, causes, identification techniques, psychological and technological factors, and recommended countermeasures for misinformation (including fact-checking, prebunking, crowdsourcing, platform interventions, and media literacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and distinction: misinformation, disinformation, malinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Misinformation is incorrect or misleading information. Disinformation is deliberately deceptive and intentionally propagated. Malinformation is true information intended to cause harm (e.g., selectively publicizing a politician's personal information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes intent and effect as distinguishing features but notes the distinction can be muddy because intent is often difficult to discern. Examples and consequences (e.g., undermining trust) are provided. Use these definitions when classifying content; expect overlap and contextual variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content characteristics of misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Misinformation can include inaccurate, incomplete, misleading, or false information as well as selective or half-truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that misinformation may be unintentional (lack of knowledge, error, misunderstanding) and that social media design enables rapid posting and sharing. When evaluating content, consider incompleteness, selective omission, and whether material is presented as fact vs opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors influencing susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Susceptibility arises from individual, group, and societal factors including cognitive biases, emotional responses, social dynamics, media literacy levels, in-group bias, echo chambers, political polarization, economic inequalities, and declining trust in science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents specific mechanisms (e.g., confirmation bias, motivated reasoning, illusory truth effect, novelty and emotional resonance) and demographic factors (age, education, digital literacy). Use these factors to assess audience vulnerability and to target interventions appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: SIFT method (Stop, Investigate, Find better coverage, Trace)
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-move method to distinguish reliable from unreliable information: Stop (ask about what you're reading/viewing), Investigate (source expertise and agenda), Find better coverage (seek reliable coverage and consensus), Trace (trace claims/quotes/media to original context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each move is a practical step: Stop to avoid impulsive sharing; Investigate to assess expertise/agenda; Find to compare coverage and consensus; Trace to check original context and omitted information. SIFT is taught as a taught method for readers and educators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for identifying visual and data-based misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual misinformation can be detected by examining misleading graphs and charts (e.g., truncated axes, poor color choices), reverse image searching to find original contexts, and current methods for identifying AI-generated imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives examples (truncated axes, misleading images increasing believability) and warns that AI-generated imagery detection is currently possible sometimes but will likely become harder. Employ reverse image search, inspect data presentation, and be cautious with images that appear to 'evidence' a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating source credibility and plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should evaluate source credibility and motivation, and consider the plausibility of claims when judging whether information is misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes common pitfalls—hyperlinks and images can increase perceived trustworthiness even if the sources are weak; readers often do not click links. Consider source expertise, possible agendas, and whether claims align with established evidence before accepting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of effective corrective messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective corrective messages depend on an individual's mental model/worldview, repetition, the timing of correction, the credibility of sources, coherency of the corrective message, and whether the original source delivers the correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrective messages are more effective when coherent and consistent with the audience's worldview; they are less effective when misinformation is repeated before correction, when there's a time lag, or when the misinformation appears to come from a credible source. Delivering corrections from the original source tends to be more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social correction best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When correcting misinformation on social platforms, corrections should include a link to a credible source, repeat the correct information (e.g., at beginning and end), and provide an alternative explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: a corrective message about chili peppers and COVID-19 that repeats the correct advice, gives an alternative explanation, and links to WHO. The article warns social correction can reach observers but may also amplify the original post; tone affects the target's reception but less so observers'.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-on-one correction strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal interactions are more likely to change beliefs when the corrector has close social ties; strategies emphasizing empathy, encouraging reflection, and instilling doubt can be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain presentation of facts is frequently ineffective. Tone matters: expressing empathy and understanding can keep communication channels open. Use relational trust and non-confrontational approaches to increase receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourced fact-checking design criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: For crowdsourced interventions to be effective, a balance of three factors is necessary: Trust (users must trust the crowd), Cognitive Dissonance (corrections must differ enough from prior beliefs to prompt update), and Crowd Size (sufficiently large and diverse group needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes aggregated judgments of a politically balanced lay crowd can be as accurate as professionals. It warns of trade-offs (in-group trust vs dissonance) and recommends approaches like the 'two steps away' network to connect audiences with slightly outside communities to maximize trust and dissonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prebunking / inoculation approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Prebunking aims to 'inoculate' people by showing examples of misinformation and the tactics used before they encounter it, focusing on identifying logical fallacies and manipulative tactics rather than only fact-based corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prebunking trains people to recognize emotional appeals, false dichotomies, ad hominem and other fallacies; research shows promising results. This is a preventive strategy to reduce susceptibility prior to exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and algorithmic interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform measures include algorithmic fact-checkers, user flagging, supplemental information in search results, warning prompts, and limits on forwarding; algorithms often amplify emotionally charged misinformation and platforms have added detection and flagging features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites Google, Facebook and others adding automatic fact-checking and warning systems but notes controversy—such efforts can be criticized as barriers to expression and may drive communities to other corners of the internet. Consider trade-offs between speed, accuracy, free expression, and potential censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal Society proposed countermeasures (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-exhaustive list of potential countermeasures: automated detection systems; provenance-enhancing technology; APIs for research; active bystanders; community moderation; anti-virals (forward limits); collective intelligence (e.g., Wikipedia); trustworthy institutions and data; and media literacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report recommends building resilience and a healthy information environment rather than removing offending content, warning that censorship could push communities to harder-to-address corners. The list serves as design criteria for multi-layered interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and challenges in misinformation research and interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Research often focuses on efficacy in lab settings rather than real-world effectiveness; challenges include overabundance of lab research, testing effects that impede longevity and scalability, modest effects for limited audiences, reliance on item-evaluation tasks, low replicability in the Global South, and potential unintended consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caution when extrapolating lab results to field conditions. Intervention design should account for scalability, cultural/contextual differences, and the risk that some countermeasures may have adverse side effects (e.g., amplifying misinformation or restricting legitimate expression).

rubrics_metrics.name: AI, synthetic media, and automation: risks and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial intelligence contributes to new types of misinformation (synthetic media, deepfakes, speech synthesis) and can both intensify fake news and be used to detect and counter misinformation. AI systems (LLMs) can hallucinate and generate false information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include AI-generated images of the Hollywood sign on fire and LLM hallucinations in legal filings. The page notes detection is sometimes possible but will become harder; national responses and detection institutions are emerging. Consider both mitigation (detection, provenance) and the risk of AI-driven amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media literacy and education as countermeasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Media literacy (information literacy) education—teaching citizens to find, evaluate, create, and communicate information—is proposed as an essential, long-term countermeasure (examples: Estonia's K–12 program; New Jersey K–12 mandate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article points to 'inoculation' educational videos for adults and school curricula as ways to build resilience. Media literacy should be tailored by age and context; it's framed as a systemic, preventive approach rather than a short-term fix.
